Another chilly night is ahead as surface high pressure builds 
southeastward from the Upper Midwest. This will lead to favorable 
radiational cooling conditions as winds decouple and become near 
calm by Sunday morning. Most areas will dip to around or below 
freezing, so a Freeze Warning remains in effect areawide Sunday

fairly widespread freeze this morning and right around the 
climatological first freeze, this will likely lead to the end of our 
fall frost/freeze program for this season. With that said, a few 
typically overtly warmer spots like ATL airport and some spots in 
Middle Georgia could technically miss the freezing mark by a degree 
or two.

the forecast period. Highs on Sunday will remain below normal but 
will rise a few degrees over today's values. Another chilly night 
will then be in store for Sunday night into Monday morning, bringing 
lows ranging from the upper 20s to mid 30s.

trough that provided a chilly weekend will finally get kicked off to 
the northeast as a shortwave slides from the Southern Plains into

south in its track, bringing rain chances down to under 10% across

a ridge will build from the Gulf up across the Southeast US during 
the second half of the week and into next weekend. Our stretch of 
dry weather will continue in this setup, and temperatures will warm 
up to around 10F above normal. Highs will climb back into the 70s

.SHORT TERM...
(Tonight through Sunday night)
Issued at 120 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Morning round of mostly elevated rains have weakened and shifted 
SE to mostly en the impacts of a passing shortwave moving over TX.
The onset of the next round of rain is trending much faster
though, as satellite and model data are bringing a jet steak
diving SE into TX. Already the low level moisture has been primed
a bit from the early day shortwave and enough moisture is coming
together to generate some streamer convection in advance of the
jet streak and deepening upper trough. The jet streak is helping
to shape a positive tilt to the digging trough as it arrives,
giving the region a boost in convective potential for tonight into
Sunday. Initially the blended guidances, while showing fairly 
high PoPs for tonight's rain chances, characterized the rains this
evening as just some showers without upper support or low level 
focus to enhance QPF. The last few hours of rapid refresh data 
reveals an uptick in evening activity not seen in the coarser 
scale models, with the RRFS showing still mostly shower activity 
over central and eastern counties and the HRRR runs showing a 
slightly deeper convective potential capable of an isolated storm 
or two with some cells dumping well over half an inch in a short 
period. The scattered streamer activity is displaying the hint of 
deeper convection potential with a couple cells lighting up with a
50 dbz echo on radar. Thus we'll be updating the current forecast
shortly to add an isolated mention of thunder to evening grids 
which had none in the midday populate and publish. 

As we were already expecting marginal risk severe potential (level
1 of 5) for Sunday, a quick peek was taken for this evening and
tonight. Wind profiles depicted good low level shear to help the
convection deepen. The undercutting NE winds will help give any
storm that develops an elevated look, but some gusty winds,
frequent lightning and perhaps some small hail shouldn't be ruled
out. Again the evening coverage is only being adjusted to around
15 percent for the chance of thunder with most activity being a
light to moderate rain. 

At daybreak Sunday the base of the upper trough drops into West
Central TX to set up the arrival of healthy cold front as a
focusing mechanism for scattered to numerous showers and storms.
This fairly quick moving system evolves fairly early in the day
and works quickly across the area to get to our far eastern
counties by 21Z. This early onset and fast progression should help
limit the potential for severe weather to be of the isolated and
short-lived variety. The marginal (1 of 4) potential for excessive
rainfall should remain the primary concern, as well as the impacts
of lightning ans strong wind gusts to interrupt weekend outdoor 
festivities.

Much of Central TX will see conditions begin to stabilize by or
shortly after noon with significant impacts to the afternoon
temperatures with a steady or slowly falling temperature trend.
The continuation of light precipitation in this shallow layer of
cold air will only add to the apparent temperature with wind 
chills probably falling to near 40 degrees by late evening, with 
all counties on the backside of the front by this time. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday through next Saturday)
Issued at 120 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Monday continues the significant cold air advection pattern with
lots of low cloud cover and perhaps a early day round of light
rain or drizzle to help add to the chill. Monday's highs should be
the lowest of the week with the maxes mainly in the 50s to low
60s. The cloud cover will minimize nighttime cooling, and the
Tuesday morning lows are expected to be comparable to the Monday
lows. 

A shortwave upper ridge moving in the zonal pattern over TX brings
a temporary end to rain chances but doesn't appear to have enough
strength or persistent to scour out the low level moisture. So we
may get some partly cloudy skies late Monday into early Tuesday,
but mostly cloudy skies should continue provide cooling through
most of the work week. South winds return mid-week but also bring
back a thicker layer of low clouds and a slight effect of
overrunning as falling heights aloft upstream from TX translate to
weak coastal troughing over the TX coast. Temperatures should
moderate back to near seasonal norms, but rain chances will return
mainly in the form of streamer convection. By Friday, the latest 
deterministic runs depict hints of embedded shortwave activity in 
the, by then, SW flow aloft pattern, which could offer the chance 
for upscaling convection.

&&

.AVIATION...
(00Z TAFS)
Issued at 525 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Deteriorating flight conditions occur now through the overnight 
and for much of Sunday, as flight categories lower from MVFR/VFR 
down to IFR levels due to the combination of lowering ceilings, 
reduced visibilities, and rounds of rain/showers across the I-35 
terminals (KAUS, KSAT, and KSSF). Instances of LIFR could occur
as well at times, especially for the I-35 terminals. The thunder 
risk should stay low initially but peaks early to mid-morning

tapers off behind the front, the ceilings will remain low with
marginal improvement, if any. Easterly winds will continue into
Sunday before shifting more north-northeasterly behind the front
with gradual uptick in wind speeds into and through Sunday night.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Overcast conditions the rest of today give way 
to mostly sunny and breezy conditions on Sunday. Temperatures 
slightly cooler than normal through this weekend.

Skies have trended toward mostly cloudy/overcast conditions with 
modest NW breezes, in response to a rather potent shortwave 
disturbance aloft seen on satellite imagery circulating near 
Montreal. While currently dry, there are a number of light but non-
trace 1-hourly QPF amts being reported by METARs in northern New 
England; while dry weather generally prevails, a sprinkle or light 
shower are possible as this shortwave disturbance moves southward 
through Southern New England late this afternoon into early tonight. 
Any additional diurnal warming looks minimal today with the cloud 
cover and northerly breezes, in the upper 30s to the mid 40s! Early 
cloud cover and northwest breezes will keep temps from really 
dropping quickly, but decreasing clouds after midnight should bring 
lows down to the upper 20s to mid/upper 30s. 

We do expect there to be more sunshine on Sunday compared to today, 
although low-level thermal profiles still are rather cool. This 
should support better mixing with northwest gusts in the 20 to 25 
mph range, which will add a bit of a chill despite sunny conditions. 
Expect highs in the mid to upper 40s, but it will feel closer to the 
mid-30s if you're doing any hikes in the higher terrain. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Prolonged period of dry and quiet weather, with
moderating temperatures next week, yielding mild afternoons and
cool nights.

All guidance, including AI models, have large amplitude central US 
ridge this weekend slowly advecting to the East Coast next week. 
Hence, a prolong stretch of dry weather for SNE. Regarding 
temperatures, chilly to begin the week Monday, but height rises 
aloft will support warming temps and with surface high setting up 
across the OH Valley to the Mid Atlantic region, this will place SNE 
in a warming WNW flow. Given this setup, wouldn't be surprised if 
forecast highs overachieve into the mid 60s in the Wed-Fri 
timeframe! Thus, the temp theme next week will be cool highs in the 
upper 40s and lower 50s Monday, jumping into the 60s mid to late 
next week. These temps are about 10-15 degs warmer than normal for 
mid Nov.

Dew pts in the 30s along with light winds, will result in a large 
diurnal temp spread, with seasonably cool nights, as lows dip into 
the 30s for most locations. The mild daytime temps likely linger 
into Fri, before a dry cold front moves across the region Fri/Sat. 
Ensembles suggest not much of a post frontal airmass change, with 
highs only cooling back to seasonal levels, with highs in the 50s. 
Hence, mild days and cool nights will be the theme for much of next 
week.

.SHORT TERM...
(This evening through Sunday)
Issued at 1220 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

A widespread and generous rainfall event will unfold across
North and Central Texas over the next 36 hours, as a vigorous
upper level shortwave drives eastward through the Southern
Rockies today, assumes a negative tilt tonight, and ejects across
the Southern Plains on Sunday. A weaker lead wave in advance of 
the main trough is already triggering a ragged swath of light 
rain from the Texas Panhandle, southeastward into the Big Country 
of Western North Texas. Some of this activity has already leaked 
into our western counties, though rain amounts should remain light
due to an extensive dry layer in the lower atmosphere. Modest 
lower level isentropic lift is already occurring throughout our 
region, and as lifting intensifies and saturation proceeds several
thousand feet above the surface, a more extensive shield of 
showers will evolve from west to east across North Texas from 
sunset onward through the overnight hours. 

More significant forcing for ascent will arrive later tonight as
the primary shortwave exits the Rockies. Coupled with enhanced low
level moisture transport from the Gulf and increased precipitable
water content, we'll see an uptick in rainfall rates after
midnight through mid morning Sunday. At least some of the CAMs are
depicting limited amounts of elevated CAPE late tonight into
Sunday morning. Given the degree of synoptic scale forcing, 
wouldn't be surprised to hear some rumbles of thunder in some areas
later tonight, which will also enhance rainfall rates prior to 
daybreak. 

Rainfall coverage should be expansive across most of North and
Central Texas through at least midday, with many locations
receiving between 0.75 and 1.5 inches of QPF by noon. The axis of
the primary trough should be passing east of the I-35 corridor by
Sunday afternoon. Subsidence behind this trough axis will promote
a marked cessation in the rain from west to east later in the 
day, though an extensive blanket of stratocumulus cloudiness
should continue to enshroud the region into Sunday evening.  

The combination of clouds, rain, and modest low level cold
advection will lead to the chilliest daytime temperatures we've
seen in North Texas so far this fall. Afternoon highs will top out
in the lower to middle 50s in most area, though locations closer
to the Red River will struggle to climb out of the middle and
upper 40s. A steady easterly breeze will make it feel several
degrees cooler.  

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through next Friday)
Issued at 1220 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Some residual wraparound moisture and low level isentropic lift
may promote some limited shower development Sunday night, and have
thus maintained low PoPs in most areas through daybreak Monday. 
In the wake of our weekend storm system, a temporary period of mid
level ridge building will commence over the Southern Plains 
Monday morning. This ridge's stay will be relative brief, 
however, as it should slide east of our area by Tuesday afternoon,
replaced by a broad southwesterly upper level flow regime which 
will persist through the remainder of the upcoming week. The net 
effect of this pattern change will be a steady day to day warming 
trend, culminating in widespread (and unseasonably warm) highs in 
the 70s from Thursday onward into the weekend. Another opportunity
for precipitation will develop Thursday as a subtle shortwave 
swings northeastward across the area within the larger-scale 
southwesterly flow pattern. Amounts, if any, with this next system
should be lighter than tomorrow's event, with most locations 
receiving less than 0.25 inch.

was just to the east of Denver, with very light showers to its 
east and north. We still have a bit of a dry layer around 750mb

portions of the I-70 and northern I-25 corridors will see fog with

much of Tuesday. On Tuesday, an upper level trough will move onto
the West Coast. Winds at mid levels will strengthen as the 
pressure gradient tightens between the upper ridge and trough.

sending a shortwave through the area early Wednesday. Precip 
chances will increase late Tuesday in the higher terrain as the 
shortwave approaches. The shortwave will be moving rather quickly 
and the southwesterly to westerly winds aloft are not super 
favorable for our area, so impacts from this event will be rather 
limited with snow totals around an inch or less for the higher 
elevations. For the plains, a cold front is forecast to move 
through sometime Wednesday, bringing slightly cooler temps for 
Wednesday into the end of the work week. Rain chances remain low 
(<20%) for the plains with the this system.

That shortwave will quickly move off to the northeast as an upper 
low moves onto the West Coast. The progression of this upper 
low/trough Thursday into the weekend is highly uncertain. A 
couple of days ago, models had a slower moving closed low headed

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 135 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Taking a look at water vapor imagery along with satellite derived PW 
values, we can see quite the split in moisture availability. 
Currently, PW values are close to the 25th percentile (~0.58") over 
our far eastern zones. Meanwhile, over Matagorda Bay, PW values are 
already exceeding the 75% percentile (~1.31"). Unsurprisingly, we 
already have some isolated showers generally around the Matagorda 
Bay area and the adjacent coastal Gulf waters as the first upper 
level disturbances pushes into the area. The ridge axis that has 
been overhead the past couple of days is pushing its way out to the 
east. As previously mentioned, the first embedded shortwave trough 
is moving through the area this afternoon. The latest high-res model 
guidance indicates that convective coverage will gradually increase 
later this afternoon once daytime "heating" comes into play. I put 
that in parentheses for now because daytime heating for today will 
only peak into the low to maybe mid 70s right around Matagorda Bay. 
There is some modest amounts of instability off the coast, so it's 
not out of the question to see some occasional bouts of lightning. 

There will still be a layer of dry air in the mid-levels (between 
500-800mb) that this increasing moisture and lift would have to 
battle through. The best chances for rain remain west of I-45 
(closer to the Brazos River). Some isolated heavier downpours will 
be possible later this afternoon into the evening around Matagorda 
Bay. Some of the latest high-res guidance supports this and even 
shows the potential for training convection right along the coast 
near Matagorda Bay late this evening into early Sunday morning. As a 
result, WPC has outlined this area (generally west of Freeport and 
south of Edna) in a marginal risk (level 1 of 5) of excessive 
rainfall for today/tonight. Due to the increasing cloud cover and 
increasing easterly winds, high temperatures today will mostly top 
out in the upper 60s to low 70s.

The next upper level disturbance is currently pushing through the 
Four Corners region which has led to surface low pressure 
development near the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The placement of 
this surface low is important to note because it will place areas 
generally west of I-45 and south of I-10 in the warm sector. There 
remains a little bit of uncertainty on how far north this warm 
sector will extend...there is potential for this to extend past the 
I-10 corridor into Harris County for instance. There'll be quite a 
bit of shear to work with as a LLJ moves in overhead Sunday morning 
as the low tracks southeastward. 

If we take a look at updraft helicity, we see that there is 
potential for a couple of stronger updrafts to push their way into 
areas within the warm sector...which is why the exact placement of 
the warm sector is important to note. So, we'll have shear, 
instability, moisture, and plenty of lift to work with...so SPC has 
outlined areas generally south of a College Station-Conroe-Liberty 
line in a marginal risk (level 1 of 5) of severe weather on Sunday. 
Damaging winds and hail are the primary hazards, but a brief 
isolated tornado can't be ruled out. We'll go over the evolution of 
this entire event in a few paragraphs...

Heavy rainfall will also be a threat, especially as the surface low 
moves into our area along with the associated cold front. This will 
surge PW values near the MAX percentile (~1.99") along the coast. 
The overlap of climatologically high PW's and numerous sources of 
lift creates the potential for rainfall rates peaking above 2-3"/hr. 
The greatest potential of this remains south of I-10 and along the 
coast. We're still expecting widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3" 
north of I-10. South of I-10, rainfall totals peak in the 3-6" range 
with the potential for totals possibly approach 6-8" with the 
highest totals occurring right along the coast (especially near 
Matagorda Bay). 

Moderate to heavy rainfall potential begins around Matagorda Bay 
this evening. As mentioned earlier, we could see training convection 
set up going into Sunday morning which will then be followed by a 
line of strong to possibly severe thunderstorms. As a result, WPC 
has outlined areas near and south of I-10 in a slight risk (level 2 
of 4) of excessive rainfall for Sunday. Elsewhere (outside of 
portions of the Piney Woods), there is a marginal risk (level 1 of 
4) of excessive rainfall. It's worth mentioning that some of the 
high-res guidance (including the RRFS), has rainfall amounts 
exceeding 15" just offshore...so we'll continue to monitor trends to 
make sure it doesn't trend further north.

Now for a brief overview of the evolution of this event...we begin 
with isolated to scattered showers this afternoon. Some training 
convection will be possible later this evening into Sunday morning 
along the coast near Matagorda Bay. Scattered showers will be 
possible throughout the morning all over Southeast Texas, and then a 
line of storms associated with a frontal boundary will begin to push 
into the Brazos Valley in the mid to late morning hours. It will 
make it into the Houston metro area in the late morning to early 
afternoon hours, and then off of the coast in the late afternoon 
hours. The strongest of the storms (if they develop) would most 
likely occur west of I-45. 

The cold front pushes offshore Sunday evening but lingering moisture 
and lift may lead to our coolest day since mid-March on Monday! 
Lingering moisture along with lift from the nearby upper level low 
will result in scattered light rain showers persisting through 
Monday afternoon...but rain chances gradually taper out from north 
to south throughout the day. A widespread thick layer of low-level 
cloud cover will also persist throughout the day. The other part of 
that equation will be gusty northeasterly winds that prevail in the 
wake of the front throughout the day on Monday. We are expecting 
sustained winds near the Wind Advisory threshold along the coast. 
Technically, wind speeds along the barrier islands will rise enough 
later this evening to warrant the issuance of a Wind Advisory 
beginning at 6pm. For the coastal counties/zones, a Wind Advisory 
will go into effect at 9am Sunday and run through Monday afternoon. 
The barrier island Wind Advisory will run through Monday evening. 

Elevated winds, lingering cloud cover, and light rain generally 
aren't favorable for heating...so the forecast high temperatures for 
Monday have continued to trend down. Most of us will not see 
temperatures rise above 60 degrees on Monday...so mostly highs in 
the upper 50s. This will likely be our coolest day that we've 
experienced since mid-March. As far as low temperatures go, we'll 
only see those bottom out in the 40s/50s Sunday night through 
Tuesday night.

We'll see a gradual warming trend through next week as high 
temperatures rise into the 60s on Tuesday and the 70s on Wednesday 
courtesy of ridging aloft moving in. The dry pattern looks to 
persist through midweek, before slight rain chances return towards 
the end of the work week.

.DISCUSSION...Through Friday

Much calmer and drier conditions have settled in over the region 
today as brief ridging sets up for the next 24-48 hours. Satellite 
imagery this afternoon shows lingering moisture and clouds over 
Mohave County AZ and points east while the rest of the Mohave desert 
and lower Great Basin have cleared out. Current LAS ACARS soundings 
reveal a much drier airmass in place with a strong subsidence 
inversion at 700mb and a deep mixed layer below with relatively calm 
winds. While winds are much lower than they were yesterday, there 
are still some pockets of terrain enhanced W-NW winds across 
portions of North and Western Clark County and Mohave County. But 
overall a dry and benign weekend with highs in the 60s to low 70s 
for desert valleys. Similar conditions expected for the latter half 
of the weekend and into Monday; however expect clouds to be on the 
increase as upper level moisture advects in as the ridge axis pushes 
east. Cloud cover thickens on Monday resulting in temperatures 
dropping by a few degrees. Guidance today did come in a little drier 
with the next system, raising confidence that much of the day Monday 
could remain dry as well despite increased clouds. 

By Monday evening, deep troughing pushes inland along the California 
Coast with a 90 kt SSW jet out ahead of it. While there is good low 
and mid level southerly flow ahead of the trough advecting moisture 
northward, guidance today has come down on both PW and QPF, 
indicating slightly weaker moisture advection into the Mohave 
Desert. ECMWF ensemble mean PW is around 0.80" for Las Vegas; 
whereas guidance was showing upwards of 1.00" yesterday. Models 
today are also coming in a few hours slowly with the system, 
bringing precipitation into the Eastern Sierra Monday evening, 
spreading eastward into Nevada late Monday night. Greatest coverage 
of rainfall and showers looks to be across Nye and Lincoln Counties 
and higher terrain Monday night with more scattered showers likely 
over Clark County. Tuesday morning, precipitation arrives in Mohave 
County while a drying trend begins in Inyo and San Bernardino 
Counties as the trough axis pushes through. Rainfall totals from 
Monday evening into Tuesday look modest (0.01 to 0.25") for all but 
Northeast Clark Co, Mohave Co, and Lincoln Co which will range from 
0.30 to 0.5" after showers exit to the east. Currently, snow in the 
upper elevations of the Sierra from this next system looks to stay 
relatively light as the best forcing and moisture advection remain 
south and east. Additional chances for rain expected later in the 
week as another system will likely be on the heals of the departing 
one. 

Yet another trough approaches the West Coast Thursday moving inland 
by Friday bringing another round of light showers and gusty winds to 
the region. With continued systems impacting the region and an 
overall troughing pattern persisting, expect a cooling trend to 
continue for most of the week with highs near to below average.

.SHORT TERM...

Issued at 401 PM EST Sat Nov 14 2026

The first cool snap of the season is finally here! Surface and 
satellite observations show a dry, cool air mass overspreading the 
entire southeastern United States today as high pressure builds, 
while a cold front lingers across the Florida Straits. The 
interaction between the two surface features have helped maintain a 
breezy northerly surface flow across South Florida, which has 
aided in the cooling sensation this morning. In fact, temperatures
across the Florida peninsula have struggled to peak past the 
upper 60s, while dew points have remained in the 30s and 40s, 
indicative of the influence of the dry air advection over the 
region. With this setup in place, expect the cool, breezy and 
sunny conditions to prevail for the rest of the day, with zero 
chances for rainfall and barely any cloud coverage to speak of. 
Overnight temperatures will also remain chilly, dropping into the 
upper 50s along the coasts, and low 50s across the interior, 

The lingering cold front should finally fizzle out by tomorrow, 
allowing the surface high to continue building south across our 
area. As a result, winds will gradually shift from the east-
northeast, advecting some slightly moister, warmer air over the 
area. Temperatures might still remain below average, peaking in 
the mid to upper 70s, but subsidence and dry air associated with 
the high pressure area will help keep rain chances to a minimum.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through next Friday)
Issued at 401 PM EST Sat Nov 14 2026

The dry and cool post-frontal conditions seen this weekend will 
gradually warm and moisten toward the start of next week. A broad 
surface high over the eastern United States will veer winds to a 
more northeasterly flow, advecting warm moist air from the 
Atlantic waters. Thanks to this influx of moisture, temperatures 
and dewpoints will begin to climb going into early next week. High
temps in the upper 70s to low 80s will return along with 
dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s. 

Heading into the middle of next week, a northern jet appears to set 
up aloft across North Florida. This jet could pull along with it a 
shortwave trough that is forecast to develop over the southern 
Plains, resulting in an increase in PoPs and surface winds for parts 
of SoFlo. Guidance agrees on the eastward propagation of this 
mid-level shortwave feature approaching the Florida peninsula 
around midweek. An associated surface low will develop and move 
east along with the parent mid-level shortwave. As this low nears 
Florida and interacts with the surface high settled over the 
eastern CONUS, a gradual tightening the pressure gradient over the
SoFlo region will take place. Placement and intensity of the 
surface low will depend on the strength and positioning of the 
shortwave trough. Currently, GEFS, GEPS and EPS guidance suggest a
weaker and more southerly track for the shortwave, which would 
push the associated surface low further south of the SoFlo region.
Further analysis of these ensemble systems show some split within
each model's member envelope. The GEFS members appear split on 
whether the surface low will develop over the Gulf or over the 
coastal Carolina waters, which is also supported by the EPS 
ensemble membership. 

With all of these potential solutions to consider, uncertainty 
regarding the resulting sensible weather across South Florida mid-to-
late next week remains high. What is more certain is that a tighter 
pressure gradient will increase surface winds early next week, 
particularly over coastal waters, calling for a gusty week ahead 
with the potential for hazardous marine conditions. Higher rain 
chances will be likely throughout the later half next week 
regardless of the positioning of the surface low. Activity should 
mostly be confined to the eastern metros as typical coastal 
convergence sets up around mid-week. However, given the scenario 
where the surface low sets up near the Carolinas rather than over 
the eastern Gulf, increased coastal convergence and moisture 
transport could increase rain chances.

.SHORT TERM...

Issued at 157 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

The broad scale trough over the eastern one-third of the nation
will gradually continue to slide eastward allowing our upper level
pattern to become more and more progressive later today through 
Sunday. With higher heights and thicknesses, temperatures 
overnight tonight will be a touch higher than this morning and 
daytime highs on Sunday will be a touch higher as well with most 
of the region warming into the middle and upper 60s respectively. 

Late Sunday eyes shift to our north and west as a rather robust 
mid and upper low begins to dig southward over the Red River 
Valley and eventually in the northwest Gulf. At the surface, a 
low pressure or at the very least a sharp surface trough develops 
and moves moves offshore toward the central Gulf by early Monday. 
At the same time a strong surface high pressure centered over the 
Ohio River Valley will help tighten the pressure gradient 
especially over the Gulf waters. As the low continues to dive into
the central Gulf there should be enough isentropic upglide to 
help generate some shower activity, albeit rather light in terms 
of amounts. QPF gradient will be an issue right over our CWFA as 
the coastal LA has the best shot at measurable precip vs southwest
Mississippi where little may be realized late Sunday through 
Monday. 

As the system moves over the Gulf, off of the natural baroclinic
zone along the coast, the system gradually loses strengthen, and 
the upper level trough starts to flatten just a bit. That said, 
lower pressures will continue to be there as with the stronger 
pressure gradient offshore with persistent easterly flow. As for 
temperatures on Monday, with the cloudiness and slightly lower 
heights, expect temperatures to be a few degrees lower than Sunday
which is roughly 10 or so degrees cooler than average for mid 
November. As the upper level pattern transitions back to a dry 
northwesterly flow and more insolation on Tuesday, temperatures 
bounce back once more, especially as an upper level ridge tries to
build back in during the day on Tuesday. (Frye) 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday Night through Friday night) 
Issued at 157 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

The southern stream disturbance responsible for Monday's 
precipitation should continue moving east across the Gulf early 
Tuesday as upper level high pressure slides east and expands across 
the southeastern CONUS. Although the primary upper level forcing 
should be shifting away from the region, the associated surface low 
or trough may be somewhat slower to depart. Consequently, a few 
lingering showers cannot be completely ruled out Tuesday morning, 
particularly across coastal southeast Louisiana. Farther inland, dry 
conditions should return more quickly. By Tuesday afternoon, most of 
the CWA should be dry as deeper moisture become increasingly 
displaced to the east and southeast. Highs should generally range 
from the upper 60s to around 70.

By Wednesday a warming trend should become more noticeable as upper 
level ridge centered to the northeast remains in place. Look for 
highs recovering into the lower to middle 70s across much of the 
CWA. Overnight lows should also gradually increase as the very dry 
continental airmass modifies and low level moisture begins 
recovering. By Thursday, temperatures should be near to slightly 
above normal across most of the region. Looking toward Friday, the 
forecast should remain predominantly dry as upper level ridging 
continues to influence the Gulf Coast. Highs may approach the upper 
70s. (MEFFER)

as the trough axis over the rockies continues to progress closer to 
the area. A dry boundary layer will help keep things dry across 
central/eastern parts of the area until later this afternoon into 
this evening with rainfall intensities then expected to increase 
later tonight as warm advection maximizes over the area.

over the area, with forcing then waning through the afternoon as the 
low moves to our east and weakens. As far as rainfall amounts, the 
12z model guidance has made a bit of a southward shift once again, 
with some CAMs also showing a fairly sharp gradient on the northeast 
side of the precip shield as it runs into drier air to the east. Our 
latest forecast has generally 0.25-1.00" from I-40 north (with 
decreasing amounts with northward extent) and 1.00-1.50" along and

potentially making it closer to 50 degrees in north-central OK and

during the day, winds here will shift southerly and potentially get

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH MONDAY/... 
The overall progressive pattern continues to evolve, with 
midlevel water vapor imagery showing a negatively tilted shortwave
disturbance passing over the Four Corners and transient ridging 
nudging eastward/inland along the West Coast ahead of another 
upper level trough offshore. Despite PHX ACARS soundings (in 
excellent agreement with GFS bufr soundings) depicting a strong 
midlevel subsidence inversion on the backside of the shortwave 
disturbance, a vort max that 500 mb RAP analysis places over 
northern AZ at this hour, coupled with WAA ahead of a poorly 
defined near-sfc front, have supplied sufficient lift to release 
meager instability on the order of 100-300 J/kg and produce 
scattered low-topped showers over portions of Central and Eastern 
AZ, especially over the higher terrain and W/SW facing slopes. As 
the disturbance and any associated forcing slides further east of 
the forecast area, anticipate shower activity to diminish later 
this afternoon and through the evening.

Transient ridging will build into the Desert Southwest ahead of 
the next open wave trough that is expected to pass through the 
region Tuesday. This has already resulted in increases in H5 
heights aloft, currently analyzed at around 572 dam. Ensemble mean
H5 heights are advertised to peak around 580 dam as the ridge 
axis passes directly overhead late Sunday, between the 50th-75th 
percentiles of climatology for this time of year. Thermal profiles
will slowly warm in response Sunday into Monday, with ensemble 
mean 850 mb temperatures rising from 9C-10C today into a 11C-14C 
range by Monday. This should yield warming surface temperatures 
across the lower deserts, with widespread highs in the 70s on 
Sunday, then near 80F across the typically warmer spots on Monday,
2F-4F above daily normals. 

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/... 
Models remain in good agreement that an upper level trough will 
push inland along the California coast late Monday and progress
over the Desert Southwest on Tuesday, albeit in a weakening 
phase. Rain chances will return to the forecast on Tuesday with 
NBM PoPs peaking between 60-90% across South-Central AZ, while SW
AZ PoPs will range between 20-60%. Latest WPC QPF indicates 
Tuesday rain totals between 0.25"-0.50" across the Greater Phoenix
area, locally higher in thunderstorms, and close to 1.00" over 
Central AZ higher terrain to the north/northeast. However, there
is still considerable spread in the model guidance, with 25th-75th
percentile QPF ranging between a few tenths to upwards of 1.25",
focused over the higher terrain to the north/northeast of 
Phoenix. A 1-2 day break in the unsettled weather will then 
likely ensue following Tuesday, ahead of the next system.

During the latter half of the week, ensembles are pointing 
towards yet another upper level trough moving inland from the 
Pacific NW, however, there are still considerable discrepancies in
the trajectory of this followup system (how far south it will 
propagate, which will impact the moisture return and placement of
the best upper level ascent mechanisms). Due to this, confidence 
remains low for PoPs/QPF late in the work week, but at the very 
least, there is building consensus for an even cooler airmass to 
enter the region as a result of this second system. Latest NBM 
highs continue to trend towards the 60s to lower 70s by late week.
However, the spread in the model guidance increases considerably 
on Friday, with IQRs on the NBM forecast temperatures increasing 
to 8F-10F.

NW flow behind an upper low passage continues to support lake-

but with a shortwave passage tonight, precipitation may shift

accumulations below 2.5kft (i.e. PA/WV ridges), due mostly to

accumulation and the top of the mixed layer only being around
-11C. Some accumulations >0.5" were observed in eastern Tucker 
 County, which have already begun to melt.

expected, but nonetheless, all elevations below 3kft are 
expected to see mostly rain showers apart from any of the most 
intense showers capable of producing graupel. For high terrain, 
even where snow is possible, accumulations are expected to be 
minimal during the daytime with radiative effects.

Overnight, high terrain accumulations again become possible 
with surface temperatures able to cool, with the Laurels 
showing an 80% chance of non-zero accumulation, while the WV 
ridges show a 90% chance. When talking about chances of >1", 
those same chances drop to <20%. Accumulation chances again drop
off Sunday with diurnal influence before precipitation chances 
diminish Sunday night.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
A pattern shift will be in-store for the next week with high
confidence in a return to drier and warmer conditions. All 
ensemble clusters are practically in complete agreement for the 
east through next weekend, showing highs rebounding to the at 
least the upper 50s by Thursday/Friday. Uncertainty trickles in

weather continues or the ridge amplitude flattens some with some

Light winds within a early morning stable boundary layer will give 
way to modest gustiness (around 20 knots) Thursday afternoon within

.PREV DISCUSSION...
Issued at 336 PM EDT Wed Oct 7 2026

DISCUSSION...

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as 
the energetic jet stream resides mostly across Canada. Stacked low 
centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations. 

Brief but strong warm up on Saturday as strong ridging over the 
Plains advances eastward over the Great Lakes. ECMWF is a touch 
warmer (~18C at 850mb) than GFS (-16C) Saturday with strong 
southwesterly flow into the region. Current forecast is for temps to 
touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later. 

This warmup will be brief as attention the turns to TS Isaias which 
is set to make landfall over MS Friday evening then getting drawn 
northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

MARINE...

Moderate southwesterly winds gradually weaken this evening as a cold 
front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass, 
and given the rejuvenated low-level jet winds, mixing likely 
delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around 
30 knots over portions of Lake Huron Thursday afternoon, with 
marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft 
Advisory may be needed over The Thumb should confidence rise in the 
frequency of 25+ knot gusts, but any higher end gusts further north 
should be infrequent enough to preclude a Gale Warning. Mid/Upper 
Mississippi Valley high pressure then expands into the area Thursday 
night and Friday offering weaker winds with a southerly shift.

.DISCUSSION (This evening through Saturday)...
Issued at 200 PM EST Sat Nov 14 2026

Surface analysis this afternoon shows a large area of high pressure 
in place through the Mississippi Valley. Cool northwest flow was in 
place across Indiana. GOES19 shows some lake cloud steaming from 
Lake MI, pushing south across north central Indiana. Aloft, a highly 
amplified pattern was in place. A sharp omega block was in place 
with ridging over the plains states, low pressure over the northeast 
and a deep trough in place over the Pacific northwest extending into 
the intermountain west. Dew points across the area were in the lower 
30s.

Tonight...

The strong ridging aloft to the west will nudge slightly eastward. 
Indiana will continue to remain under the influence of lee side 
subsidence and NW flow aloft through the overnight hours. Meanwhile 
at the surface, the strong high pressure system will also nudge 
east, arriving over IL and WI. This will keep light NW flow across 
Indiana, but should result in clearing skies across our area as the 
lake clouds drifts farther to the northeast and heating is lost. Dew 
point depressions overnight may fall to less than 2F. This with 
clearing skies and light winds will be a good set-up for radiational 
cooling and fog. Look for overnight lows around 30.

Sunday and Monday...

The strong ridging aloft will build east across Indiana on Sunday 
and Monday. Furthermore, a secondary ridge aloft is suggested to 
develop within the pattern over the Central Plains on Monday, 
reinforcing subsidence across the area. Meanwhile within the lower 
levels, the strong surface high pressure system to west will build 
eastward, settling over Indiana and Ohio on Monday. This will bring 
more dry and cool weather to our area for this time. Forecast 
soundings on Sunday suggest that convective temperatures may be 
reached producing some flat topped stratocu, but more sunshine is 
indicated on Monday with a dry column in play. Thus a partly cloudy 
Sunday and mostly sunny Monday will be in store. Slight warm air 
advection is indicated for Sunday and Monday. Thus highs around 50 
on Sunday should warm to the lower 50s for Monday. These values are 
at or below seasonal normals.

Tuesday through Saturday...

Surface high pressure positioned over the central CONUS will slowly 
settle into the region through the week. Deep subsidence and 
increasing heights from the subsequent surface high will keep skies 
mostly clear through late Wednesday. During the day Wednesday, a 
subtle shortwave trough will start to take shape over the Great 
Plains. A subsequent surface low pressure system is expected to form 
over the Nebraska/South Dakota vicinity with a cold front extending 
south towards the MO River Valley. While the subsequent surface low 
will remain well north of central Indiana, subtle isentropic ascent 
will promote the development of SCT to BKN mid to high level clouds

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH MONDAY NIGHT/...

The region is located between an upper level low moving off
towards the northeastern CONUS and another upper level trough 
moving southeast towards the southern Plains currently. A 
cooler air mass remains over the region as highs today will warm
into the upper 40s to the lower 50s this afternoon. A dry air

to 40% range today. Light east to southeasterly winds will occur

southeast across the southern Plains tonight into Sunday then
slowly to the southeast on Monday remaining south of the area.
A drier air mass is in place across the area and the better lift
will remain southwest of the area so no rain is expected across
the area with this system. 

High level clouds will continue to move east across the area 
today into Sunday morning. Clear skies are then expected Sunday
night through Monday night. Highs will warm a few degrees each
day with highs in the lower to middle 50s on Sunday with highs
in the middle 50s to near 60 on Monday. The NBM has a small
temperatures spread in highs between the ensemble model members
through Monday. Afternoon RH values will again drop to around 30
to 40% with light southeasterly winds both Sunday and Monday.

Surface highs pressure will remain over the region through
Monday then will start to push off to the east Monday night.
Lows tonight and again Sunday night will again drop into the 
lower 20s to the lower 30s with the coldest readings across the 
eastern Ozarks. Lows Sunday night into Monday morning may
actually be a few degrees cooler than tonight as high level
clouds will be in place tonight. Lows on Monday night into
Tuesday morning will range from the middle/upper 20s across the
eastern Ozarks to the upper 30s across extreme southeastern
Kansas as southerly winds start return from west to east.

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 108 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Tuesday through Thursday:

Long wave charts indicate that an upper-level ridge will be 
positioned over the region during the midweek period. Ensemble 
clusters are consistent in bringing an upper-level short wave 
trough out of the western U.S. and into the northern and central
Plains on Wednesday before reaching the western Great Lakes 
early Thursday. This feature will likely be shearing with time 
given that it will encounter the long wave ridge.

At the surface, a sprawling area of high pressure will remain
entrenched over the eastern U.S. That aforementioned short wave
trough will be reflected at the surface in the form of a cold
front. However, the track and shearing nature of the wave will
likely result in that front either remaining north of the area
or being very weak in nature if it can manage to pass through
the Ozarks.

Given an overall lack of forcing and limited moisture return,
it will be difficult to realize any measurable precipitation. We
have kept PoPs in the 10-20% range from Wednesday night into
Thursday if forcing and moisture return are on the higher end of
the ensemble envelope.

NBM probabilistic data reveals tight clustering with respect to
temperatures for the midweek period, thus our confidence is high
in temperature forecasts. High temperatures will return to the
middle 60s to lower 70s by Thursday.

Friday into Monday:

Ensembles indicate a stronger upper level short wave trough
emerging from the Rockies and into the central U.S. However, the
timing and magnitude of this wave vary considerably. We are
confident that this wave will be stronger than the feature that
passes through the region around midweek as the long wave ridge
is forecast to weaken over the central U.S. by the weekend.

With that being said, a cold front will likely pass through the
area sometime in the Friday night or Saturday time frame.
Stronger forcing and better moisture return will both be favored
with this setup, thus we expect the potential for showers and
perhaps a few thunderstorms with the frontal passage. The
potential for thunder will depend on the quality of moisture
return and overall instability. For now, we have PoPs in the
30-50% range from late Friday night into Saturday night. PoPs
may be increased for a specific time period once we get a better
feel for the timing of that cold front.

Temperatures ahead of that front will continue to be mild on
Friday with highs ranging from the upper 60s to middle 70s.
Temperatures will then cool off behind the front, however the
magnitude of cooling behind the front for Sunday and early next
week is still in question:

Scenario 1 (60% chance): Ensemble clusters indicate 
northwesterly flow developing behind the trough with a stronger 
polar fetch. This would result in a more substantial cooldown 
with highs in the upper 40s to middle 50s and lows in the upper 
20s to middle 30s.

Scenario 2 (40% chance): Ensemble clusters indicate a flatter 
flow behind the passing trough and less in the way of a polar 
fetch. This would result in a more modest cooldown with highs 
falling back into the upper 50s to middle 60s with lows in the 
middle 30s to lower 40s.

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 128 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Broad troughing aloft is leftover in the wake of the midweek storm 
system. While the core of the trough continues through New England 
today, expansive surface high pressure behind it continues to spread 
across the central US, with its axis near the Mississippi 
River. This has led to clear and cool conditions. Despite 
plenty of sun, temperatures have only reached into the mid to
upper 40s today at the time of writing. With the surface high 
keeping winds calm tonight, we'll see another good radiational 
cooling night, with the cold spots dropping into the low 20s. 
There is, however, a little bit of cloud cover stemming from a 
trough traversing the Four Corners and heading into Texas. This 
little bit of high level cloudiness could keep our southwestern 
portions from dropping as cold as last night. But if conditions 
remain clear all night, we'll be just as cold as this morning.

While the surface high reaches the Mississippi River this evening, 
it will remain dominant over our region for several more days as it 
slowly moves east toward the Ohio Valley. The result for us will be 
a gradual air mass moderation in place with daily sunshine helping 
to take the bite out of this Arctic air mass. However, clear and 
calm nights will lead to continued freezes even as daytime highs 
nudge back into the upper 50s to 60 degrees by Tuesday.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 128 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

Quiet and dry weather continues at least through midweek as the 
upper level ridge builds over the Mississippi Valley and the 
surface high drifts across the Ohio Valley and into the Mid Atlantic 
Region.  Highs warm up to near seasonal normals in the mid 50s by 
Monday, and then further into the upper 50s Tuesday, and then 60s on 
Wednesday and Thursday as southerly flow increases ahead of the next 
upstream short wave. Global guidance shows little moisture return 
through at least Tuesday with ridging over the eastern 1/2 of the 
CONUS blocking the Gulf, so the sky should remain clear to mostly 
clear through that period. The clear sky and continuing light winds 
overnight will allow temperatures to fall into the 20s again Monday 
and Tuesday mornings in most locations.  However, increasing 
southerly flow on the western side of the surface ridge will keep 
temperatures from falling as much on Wednesday morning except in 
sheltered locations.  Then there should be some moisture return into 
the region Wednesday and Wednesday night as a short wave crosses the 
Rockies and forces cyclogenesis over the Plains. Deterministic 
guidance is in pretty good agreement up to that point in the 
forecast, but begins diverging Thursday into Friday.  There's 
disagreement between the GFS and ECMWF on the amplitude and 
orientation of the short wave as it moves from the Plains into the 
Midwest Wednesday night into Thursday.  This leads to differences in 
the strength of the surface low, how far southeast the associated 
cold front travels, and how much moisture is pulled up into the Mid 
Mississippi Valley ahead of it.  The GFS is largely dry for Thursday 
and Friday, but the ECMWF is showing stronger moisture return and 
prints out around 1/2 an inch of QPF. About 20-30 percent of the 
LREF members have precip for our area which agrees well with the 
latest NBM forecast.  Therefore chance PoPs for the end of the 
forecast period continue to look reasonable, along with temperatures 
warming well above normal in southwest flow ahead of the front.
